newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - United sets push into NZ homes. [CORRECTED 05:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - United sets push into NZ homes. [CORRECTED 05:50 GMT]

text.p: UIH Asia/Pacific Communications Inc wants to be the major domestic telecommunications competitor in New Zealand through its Saturn cable unit, chief operating officer John Porter said on Friday.

Speaking after the signing of an interconnect agreement between Saturn and market giant Telecom New Zealand, Porter said Saturn's ambitious NZ$600 million 10-year plan for New Zealand reflected the Australasian thrust of its U.S. parent United International Holdings Inc's foray into the Asia-Pacific market.
Two years ago UIH launched its AUSTAR direct-to-home TV service in Australia, but Saturn offers telephony and data too.
Commenting on the capital-intensive business of cabling streets in urban centres, as Saturn has started doing in New Zealand, Porter said multi-media options justified the risk.

He told Reuters the higher investment in cabling, compared to single products like satellite TV delivery or toll call services, could also offer higher returns "in the area of convergence of telephony, video and data".
Saturn is laying fibre optic cable around Wellington and plans to launch its telephone service in early 1998.
Porter said that within weeks it would launch Saturn Home Cinema, an on-demand movie system.
"It's the first time we've applied this technology in our region (and) we're using digital file servers that provide superb picture quality and reliability," he said.
He called data services, including high-speed modem and internet connections, another revenue stream that had "a tremendous amount of upside and revenue potential".
Asked if the company would emphasise telephony as a profit source he said, "long-term, the telephony product would contribute more to the bottom line".
However, at the initial stage, part of its competitive edge would be the ability to offer a variety of bundled services.

Although Saturn is not yet revealing how many homes it expects to pass or what sort of penetration rates it expects for its various services, Porter said the plan of attack would be to expand in main centres with Christchurch then Auckland next.
"(Expansion) is contingent on the success we have with our competitive packages, but we hope to be the ubiquitous network in the larger cities."

In this respect, he noted, Saturn was taking a head-to-head competitive stance against the dominant player in New Zealand, in the same way internationally-backed Optus was doing in the Australian market against state-owned Telstra Corp.
"Our strategy with Saturn in New Zealand (facing Telecom) is the same as Optus in Australia," Porter said.
As for performance, he said he hoped Saturn could show positive ebitda earnings as quickly as AUSTAR had managed.
"We think we can be ebitda positive in a reasonably short time. In Australia we were ebitda positive by the fourth quarter and we launched 24 months ago."
"It (AUSTAR) is very successful, it has 150,000 customers paying an average of A$43 per month, and is adding about 10,000 subscribers a month," Porter noted.
He predicted that, as has happened with AUSTAR this year, Saturn would seek its own long-term debt financing in due course.

And he added, "over time we'll be looking at the long-term capital structure of this business", though it was too early to say if seeking partners or raising equity market capital for national or regional business would be the preferred route.

During Friday the Herald newspaper reported that New Zealand's main direct-to-home pay-television company Sky TV, controlled by a consortium dominated by Bell Atlantic and Ameritech Holdings, was weighing an NZ$800 million float.
(Corrects from "Sky TV, half-owned by INL, an affiliate of Australia's News Corp").
